claims.text: Medical collection debt under $500 is left off credit reports under the bureaus' policy, even if unpaid and in collection; effective spring 2023
claims.quote: Omitting any medical debt under $500 on credit reports. Medical debts under $500 will never be reported even if unpaid and even if in collection.  This change took effect in the Spring of 2023.

claims.text: Paid medical debt is removed from credit reports
claims.quote: Removing paid medical debt from credit reports, so that there would be no indications that these debts were ever in default;

claims.text: Medical debt is not reported until it has been delinquent for at least a year
claims.quote: Refraining from including medical debt in credit reports if the debt is less than one year delinquent;

claims.text: The three nationwide bureaus agreed in 2022 to three voluntary changes; NCLC's Sept 21, 2026 update still tells consumers to check compliance with them
claims.quote: Consumers should regularly order a free report from each of the nationwide CRAs to ensure that the CRAs are complying with these voluntary policies and with the state limits described below.

claims.text: Bureaus agreed in 2022 to three changes
claims.quote: In 2022, nationwide CRAs agreed to three changes to reduce the amount of medical debt in credit reports:

claims.text: Free reports from the central source, AnnualCreditReport.com; bureaus still offer free reports weekly rather than the once a year the FCRA requires
claims.quote: The nationwide CRAs also continue to offer free credit reports once a week instead of once a year as required by the FCRA.

claims.text: AnnualCreditReport.com is the central source for free reports
claims.quote: one should obtain a free credit report from the central source ... Consumers can obtain the report from the central source in any of these ways: Order online at www.annualcreditreport.com/index.action

claims.text: NCLC says the court's decision vacates the rule nationwide (no federal ban)
claims.quote: The court granted the motion to vacate the rule in its entirety. ... The impact of the court’s decision is to vacate the rule nationwide

claims.text: Unpaid medical collection over $500 more than a year delinquent can still appear; under $500, paid or recent generally does not
claims.quote: Refraining from including medical debt in credit reports if the debt is less than one year delinquent; Removing paid medical debt from credit reports ... Omitting any medical debt under $500 on credit reports.

claims.text: Oct 28, 2025 CFPB interpretive rule says it is not binding and courts decide (supporting ref 13)
claims.quote: By its own admission, the 2025 interpretive rule states it is not legally binding and the question is fundamentally one for the courts to decide.

claims.text: As of the Sept 21, 2026 update, 15 states and DC limit medical debt reporting, including CA, CO, MN, NJ, NY
claims.quote: Fifteen States and the District of Columbia Limit Medical Debt Reporting

claims.text: Case law on preemption is mixed
claims.quote: While the case law and CFPB opinions have been mixed on the preemption issue

claims.text: First Circuit held in 2022 that FCRA did not preempt Maine's earlier medical debt reporting law
claims.quote: Consumer Data Indus. Ass’n v. Frey, 26 F.4th 1 (1st Cir. 2022), which held that the FCRA does not preempt Maine’s law restricting the reporting of medical debt

claims.text: A Texas federal court held in August 2026 that the FCRA preempts a Texas law on reporting debts from surprise medical bills
claims.quote: CDIA v Paxton, 2026 WL 2322668 (W.D. Tex. Aug. 10, 2026) held that the FCRA preempts a Texas law prohibiting the reporting of debts from surprise medical bills

claims.text: Rule vacated July 2025, so bureau policies and state laws are what limit reporting (FAQ)
claims.quote: the Big Three credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) have taken voluntary actions to eliminate some medical debt. ... a federal district court in Texas struck down the rule.

claims.text: Medical collection debt with an initial reported balance under $500 removed from credit reports as of April 2023
claims.quote: The Nationwide Credit Reporting Agencies (NCRAs) — Equifax®, Experian® and TransUnion® — removed medical collection debt with an initial reported balance of under $500 from U.S. consumer credit reports as of April 2023.

claims.text: Equifax says the under-$500 change removes nearly 70 percent of collection accounts from consumer credit files
claims.quote: This change in credit reporting removes nearly 70 percent of collection accounts from consumer credit files.

claims.text: Paid medical collection debt removed effective July 1, 2022; one-year wait before unpaid medical collection debt appears; changes made in 2022
claims.quote: follows changes made by the NCRAs in 2022. Effective July 1, 2022, paid medical collection debt is no longer included on U.S. consumer credit reports.

claims.text: One-year wait gives time to work with provider or insurer
claims.quote: the time period before unpaid medical collection debt appears on a consumer’s report was increased from 6 months to one year, giving consumers more time to work with insurance and/or healthcare providers

claims.text: When a bill looks wrong, contact the provider and insurer
claims.quote: If you believe you've found an error, contact your medical provider or health insurance company.

claims.text: You can dispute a medical collection listed by mistake with the bureaus
claims.quote: If you believe that a debt has been listed on your credit report mistakenly, contact the medical provider or collection agency first. You can also file a dispute with the three NCRAs.

claims.text: Unpaid medical collections over $500 can appear and hurt your score if unpaid after the 365-day grace period
claims.quote: Medical bills over $500 will appear on your credit report and negatively impact your credit score if your account is sold to collections and you don't pay the bill within the 365-day grace period.

claims.text: One-year wait runs from the delinquency date
claims.quote: the three main consumer credit bureaus give you a 365-day grace period after the delinquency date to pay the debt before adding the collection account to your credit report.

claims.text: Can remain seven years after becoming delinquent, but removed once paid
claims.quote: Unpaid medical collection accounts over $500 can remain on your credit report for seven years after becoming delinquent; however, they will be removed once you pay the debt.

claims.text: Newer VantageScore models do not consider unpaid medical collections at all
claims.quote: newer FICO credit scoring models give less weight to unpaid medical collections than to other types of collections, and newer VantageScore® credit scoring models don't consider unpaid medical collections at all.
